gloss: Anything people or animals eat to stay alive.
examples: We spent way too much on *food* this month.
The *food* at that place is nothing special.
There's plenty of *food* in the fridge.

gloss: An occasion when food is eaten, such as breakfast or dinner.
examples: Dinner is the only *meal* we eat together.
He hasn't had a hot *meal* in days.

gloss: The first meal of the day, eaten in the morning.
examples: They serve *breakfast* until eleven on weekends.
We had eggs and toast for *breakfast*.
contrast: Written break + fast but said BREK-fuhst — the first syllable rhymes with wreck, not with brake.

gloss: A meal eaten in the middle of the day.
examples: She brings *lunch* from home every day.

gloss: The main meal of the day, usually eaten in the evening.
examples: They invited us over for *dinner* on Saturday.

gloss: A light evening meal, especially one eaten late.
examples: My grandmother still calls the evening meal *supper*.
We had soup and bread for *supper*.
The kids get a snack before *supper*.

gloss: A late-morning meal that takes the place of both breakfast and lunch.
examples: We're meeting friends for *brunch* on Sunday.

gloss: A small amount of food eaten between meals.
examples: Grab a *snack* before we head out.
The kids need *snacks* for the road trip.
I keep *snacks* in my desk drawer.

gloss: Sweet food served at the end of a meal.
examples: She made a chocolate cake for *dessert*.
contrast: Two s's and stress on the second syllable — dih-ZURT. With one s, desert (DEZ-urt) is the sandy place.

gloss: A small dish served before the main course.
examples: We ordered a couple of *appetizers* to share.
The wings are the best *appetizer* here.
*Appetizers* are half price during happy hour.
contrast: Americans say appetizer; the British say starter.

gloss: One of the separate parts of a meal, served one after another.
examples: Dinner was three *courses* and took two hours.
Soup came first, then the fish *course*.
contrast: Sounds exactly like coarse (грубый) — only the spelling differs.

gloss: A particular kind of prepared food.
examples: Each of us brought a *dish* to the potluck.
The menu has a few vegetarian *dishes*.

gloss: A set of instructions for cooking a particular dish.
examples: Can you send me the *recipe* for that soup?
I followed the *recipe* exactly and it still came out flat.
She has a whole box of her mother's *recipes*.
contrast: Three syllables, RES-uh-pee — the final e is pronounced, so it does not rhyme with ripe.

gloss: One of the foods that go into a dish.
examples: You only need five *ingredients* for this.

gloss: The amount of food served to one person.
A meal where guests serve themselves from a table of dishes.
examples: The hotel puts out a breakfast *buffet*.
He went back to the *buffet* three times.
*Buffets* are cheaper for a big group.
contrast: The final t is silent and the stress falls on the second syllable — buh-FAY.

gloss: A meal eaten outdoors, away from home.
examples: We had a *picnic* by the lake.
They pack the same *picnic* every year.

gloss: Food that remains after a meal and is eaten later.
contrast: Used only in the plural as a noun; before another noun it drops the s — leftover pizza.

gloss: The main dish of a meal in an American restaurant.
examples: The *entrées* all come with a side salad.
He picked the cheapest *entrée* on the menu.
contrast: In the US an entrée is the main course; in France and Britain it is the starter.

gloss: Cooked food bought at a restaurant to eat somewhere else.
examples: She orders *takeout* three nights a week.
contrast: Americans say takeout; the British say takeaway.

gloss: A basic food that people eat regularly and depend on.
examples: Rice is a *staple* in half the world.
Bread and potatoes were the *staples* of his childhood.

gloss: A powder made by grinding grain, used for baking.
examples: Add the *flour* a little at a time.
This bread is made with whole wheat *flour*.
contrast: Pronounced exactly like flower (цветок) — FLOW-ur.

gloss: A grain used to make most bread and pasta.
examples: This bread is made from whole *wheat*.

gloss: A tall grain plant with large yellow kernels, eaten as a vegetable.
examples: The fields around here are all *corn*.
Add a can of *corn* to the soup.
contrast: In the US corn means кукуруза; the British call that maize, and their corn means grain in general.

gloss: A grain used to make dark bread, and the bread made from it.
examples: *Rye* grows in poorer soil than wheat.
The *rye* has caraway seeds in it.
contrast: One syllable, RY — a homophone of wry.

gloss: A hot breakfast dish made from oats cooked in water or milk.
examples: Put some brown sugar on your *oatmeal*.
The *oatmeal* got cold while we talked.
contrast: Americans say oatmeal; the British call the same dish porridge.

countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings
gloss: Breakfast food made from grain, or a grain crop.
examples: We're out of milk, so no *cereal*.
Wheat and rice are the world's main *cereals*.
contrast: Sounds exactly like serial (серийный) — SEER-ee-uhl.

gloss: Food made from flour and water in shapes such as spaghetti or penne.
examples: Cook the *pasta* until it's just tender.
There's a great *pasta* place near the office.
contrast: Americans say PAH-stuh; the British say PASS-tuh.

gloss: A long thin strip of pasta or dough, usually boiled.
examples: The soup is mostly broth and *noodles*.
He ate a whole bowl of *noodles*.

gloss: Pasta in the form of long thin strings.
examples: He twirled the *spaghetti* around his fork.
contrast: Uncountable in English — the spaghetti is ready, never are ready.

gloss: A living substance used to make bread rise.
examples: The recipe calls for a packet of *yeast*.
The *yeast* was dead, so nothing rose.
contrast: Uncountable and singular in English, though Russian дрожжи is plural — the yeast is fresh.

gloss: A thick mixture of flour and liquid that is baked into bread.
examples: Let the *dough* rise for an hour.
The *dough* was too sticky to work with.
She rolled the *dough* into a ball.
contrast: The ough is a plain OH — DOH, exactly like doe.

gloss: A thin liquid mixture of flour, eggs, and milk used for frying or baking.
examples: Pour the *batter* into the hot pan.
The *batter* should be smooth, not lumpy.

gloss: Bread that has been browned by heat.
examples: The *toast* burned while I was on the phone.
She had *toast* with jam for breakfast.
contrast: Uncountable — a piece of toast, never a toast. A toast means тост-здравица.

gloss: Two slices of bread with a filling between them.
examples: I packed a *sandwich* for the trip.
contrast: The d is usually dropped in speech — SAN-wich.

gloss: A small round bread roll, often sweet or used for a sandwich.
examples: The burger *buns* are in the freezer.
She warmed the *buns* in the oven.

gloss: A dense ring-shaped bread roll that is boiled before it is baked.
examples: I'll take a *bagel* with cream cheese.
The *bagels* here are the real thing.
He toasted half a *bagel* for breakfast.

gloss: A small sweet cake baked in a cup-shaped mold.
examples: I grabbed a *muffin* on the way in.

gloss: A light, flaky crescent-shaped roll of buttery pastry.
examples: He had a *croissant* and black coffee.
contrast: A French word: the stress is on the second syllable — kruh-SAHNT, not KROY-sant.

gloss: A small ring of sweet fried dough.
examples: There's one *doughnut* left in the box.
contrast: The ough is just OH — DOH-nut. Usually spelled donut in the US.

gloss: A thin flat cake of batter fried on both sides.
A crisp batter cake baked in a grid-patterned iron.
examples: The hotel has a *waffle* maker at breakfast.

gloss: A small flat sweet baked cake.
examples: The *cookies* are still in the oven.
She sent us a tin of homemade *cookies*.
contrast: Americans say cookie; the British call it a biscuit.

gloss: A thin, dry, salty baked wafer.
examples: We had cheese and *crackers* before dinner.
The *crackers* went soft in the humidity.
He crumbled a *cracker* into his soup.

gloss: A sweet baked food made from flour, sugar, eggs, and fat.
examples: She made a carrot *cake* for his birthday.
There's still half a *cake* on the counter.
Would you like a piece of *cake*?

gloss: A baked dish of fruit or meat inside a pastry crust.
examples: My mom makes an apple *pie* every fall.

countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings
gloss: Dough of flour, fat, and water used for baking, or a sweet item made from it.
examples: He picked a *pastry* from the case.

gloss: The hard outer layer of bread, or the pastry shell of a pie.
examples: He always leaves the *crust* on his plate.
The bread has a nice thick *crust*.

gloss: A tiny piece of bread or cake that breaks off.
examples: There were *crumbs* all over the counter.
He brushed the *crumbs* off his shirt.
contrast: The b is silent — KRUHM.

gloss: A thin flat round bread made from corn or wheat flour.
examples: Warm the *tortillas* before you fill them.
He wrapped the eggs in a *tortilla*.
The *tortillas* come twelve to a pack.
contrast: The ll is said like y — tor-TEE-uh, never tor-TILL-uh.

gloss: A soft yellow fat made from cream, spread on bread or used in cooking.
A solid food made from milk.
examples: There's *cheese* and crackers in the kitchen.
He put extra *cheese* on the pizza.

gloss: The oval object laid by a hen, eaten as food.
examples: He cracked an *egg* into the pan.

gloss: A thick, slightly sour food made from fermented milk.
examples: She has *yogurt* and fruit for breakfast.
Grab a couple of *yogurts* while you're there.
contrast: Americans say YOH-gurt; the British say YOG-urt and often spell it yoghurt.

gloss: The thick fatty part of milk.
examples: Do you take *cream* in your coffee?
Whip the *cream* until it holds a peak.

gloss: Milk and the foods made from it.
examples: The *dairy* aisle is in the back.
contrast: DAIR-ee. Do not mix it up with diary (DY-uh-ree, дневник) — the letters are nearly the same.

gloss: A sweet spread made by boiling fruit with sugar.
examples: There's a jar of *jam* in the pantry.

gloss: A clear fruit spread made from strained juice, with no pieces of fruit in it.
contrast: In the US jelly is a seedless fruit spread; the wobbly British dessert called jelly is Jell-O here.

gloss: A thick sweet substance made by bees.
examples: There's a jar of *honey* in the cupboard.
contrast: The o sounds like UH — HUHN-ee, not HOH-nee.

gloss: A thick sweet liquid poured over food or added to drinks.
examples: Add a splash of *syrup* to the coffee.

gloss: A thick liquid served with or poured over food.
contrast: SAWS has no r in it — keep it apart from source (SORS).

gloss: A sauce made from the juices of cooked meat.
examples: The turkey came with *gravy* and stuffing.

gloss: A thick sweet tomato sauce eaten with fries and burgers.
A sharp yellow or brown sauce made from mustard seeds.
examples: I'll take *mustard* on that, no mayo.
The *mustard* is in the door of the fridge.

gloss: A thick pale sauce made from eggs and oil.
examples: She mixed the tuna with a little *mayonnaise*.

gloss: A sour liquid used in cooking and in salad dressing.
examples: Add a splash of *vinegar* to the dressing.
The pickles sit in *vinegar* for a week.

countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
gloss: A strong-tasting dried part of a plant used to flavor food.
examples: The *spices* are in the cabinet by the stove.
This curry has too much *spice* for me.

gloss: A plant whose leaves are used to flavor food.
examples: Basil is the only *herb* I can keep alive.
contrast: In American English the h is silent — URB, and you say an herb. The British pronounce the h.

gloss: A sweet brown spice made from tree bark.

countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings
gloss: A hot-tasting powder used to season food, or a hollow vegetable of the same name.
examples: There's too much *pepper* in this soup.

gloss: Salt, pepper, herbs, or spices added to food for flavor.
examples: The *seasoning* is what makes this dish.

countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
gloss: The particular taste of a food or drink.
examples: This soup has no *flavor* at all.
They have thirty-one *flavors* of ice cream.
The *flavor* gets stronger as it sits.
contrast: American spelling flavor; British flavour.

gloss: The food put inside a pie, sandwich, or pastry.
examples: What *filling* do you want in your omelet?

gloss: Meat from a cow.
examples: This stew takes about two pounds of *beef*.
contrast: Uncountable, and the animal has a different name: cow for the animal, beef for the meat.

gloss: Meat from a pig.
Salted or smoked meat from the leg of a pig.
examples: There's *ham* and cheese in the fridge.

gloss: Salted or smoked meat from the back or sides of a pig.
examples: He wants extra *bacon* on the burger.
contrast: Uncountable — three strips of bacon, never three bacons.

gloss: Ground meat and seasoning packed into a thin skin.
examples: He had eggs and *sausage* for breakfast.

gloss: A thick flat piece of meat, usually beef, cut for grilling or frying.
examples: How do you want your *steak* cooked?
contrast: The ea sounds like AY — STAYK, a homophone of stake (кол).

gloss: A large bird raised for food, and its meat.
examples: He made sandwiches with the leftover *turkey*.

gloss: Fish and shellfish eaten as food.
examples: The restaurant is known for its *seafood*.
We ate *seafood* every night on the coast.
contrast: Uncountable in English, though Russian морепродукты is plural — seafood is expensive, not are.

gloss: A large piece of meat cooked in an oven.
examples: She put a *roast* in the oven at noon.

gloss: A flat cake of ground beef served in a round bun.
A cooked sausage served in a long soft bun.
examples: We had *hot dogs* at the game.
He put mustard on his *hot dog*.
The stand sells *hot dogs* for two bucks.

gloss: A flat round bread baked with tomato sauce, cheese, and toppings.
examples: We split two *pizzas* between six of us.
contrast: The zz sounds like ts — PEET-suh.

gloss: A cold dish of raw vegetables, or of other foods mixed with dressing.
examples: She brought a potato *salad* to the picnic.

gloss: A dish of meat and vegetables cooked slowly in liquid.
examples: There's *stew* left over from last night.
contrast: Americans say STOO; the British say STYOO.

gloss: A thin soup made by boiling meat, fish, or vegetables in water.
examples: He lived on *broth* for a week after surgery.

gloss: A dish of food baked slowly in a deep pan.
Beaten eggs cooked flat in a pan and folded over a filling.
examples: She orders the same *omelet* every time.
contrast: American spelling omelet; British omelette. Both are said AHM-lit.

countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings
gloss: Meat cooked slowly over fire or smoke, or the outdoor party where it is served.
examples: Texas *barbecue* is a whole different thing.
We went to three *barbecues* that summer.

gloss: A small ball or pocket of dough, boiled or steamed, often with a filling.
examples: The chicken soup had *dumplings* in it.

gloss: A sandwich made by rolling a filling inside a soft flatbread.
examples: He got a chicken *wrap* for lunch.
The *wraps* are cheaper than the sandwiches.
contrast: The w is silent — RAP, exactly like the music.

gloss: A tortilla rolled around beans, rice, and meat.
examples: He can eat a whole *burrito* in five minutes.
The *burritos* here are the size of your arm.

gloss: A baked dish of flat pasta layered with sauce and cheese.
examples: The *lasagna* has to rest before you cut it.
contrast: The gn sounds like ny — luh-ZAHN-yuh. Americans spell it lasagna, the British lasagne.

gloss: A Japanese dish of vinegared rice served with raw fish or vegetables.
A dish of meat or vegetables cooked in a spiced sauce.
examples: The *curry* was hotter than I expected.

gloss: A spicy sauce of chopped tomatoes, onions, and peppers.
examples: She makes her own *salsa* in the summer.

gloss: A plant or part of a plant eaten as food.
contrast: Three syllables in speech — VEJ-tuh-buhl. The e after the g disappears.

gloss: Fresh fruit and vegetables sold in a store.
contrast: The noun is stressed on the first syllable, PROH-doos; the verb is pruh-DOOS.

gloss: A round vegetable with a strong smell, made of layers.
examples: Chop an *onion* and toss it in the pan.
She left the *onions* out of the salad.
contrast: Starts with UH, not OH — UHN-yuhn.

gloss: A strong-smelling bulb used in cooking.
The edible seed of certain plants, eaten as a vegetable.
examples: The chili has three kinds of *beans*.
He ate rice and *beans* every day.

gloss: A small round green seed eaten as a vegetable.
examples: The kids push the *peas* around their plates.

gloss: A small flat dried seed cooked as food.
A dry fruit with a hard shell and an edible kernel inside.
examples: There are mixed *nuts* on the counter.
He cracked a *nut* with his teeth.

gloss: Long thin strips of potato fried until crisp.
contrast: Almost always plural. Americans say fries; the British say chips.

gloss: A thin crisp slice of potato fried and eaten as a snack.
contrast: American chips are British crisps; what the British call chips, Americans call fries.

gloss: Corn kernels heated until they burst open, eaten as a snack.
examples: He ate an entire bucket of *popcorn*.
contrast: Uncountable — a bag of popcorn, never two popcorns.

gloss: A sweet brown food made from cacao beans.
examples: She keeps dark *chocolate* in her desk.
contrast: Two syllables in normal speech — CHAWK-lit, not cho-co-late.

gloss: Sweet food made mainly of sugar.
examples: The kids came back with bags of *candy*.
He gave up *candy* for a month.
There's a bowl of *candy* by the door.
contrast: Uncountable in the US — a piece of candy. The British say sweets, which is plural.

gloss: A sweet frozen food made from cream and sugar.
examples: We got *ice cream* after the game.
The *ice cream* melted before he finished it.
She likes *ice cream* with hot fudge.

gloss: A soft, creamy sweet dish eaten cold.
examples: The kids each got a cup of *pudding*.
contrast: In the US pudding is one specific creamy dessert; in Britain pudding can mean dessert in general.

gloss: A sweet coating spread over a cake.
examples: He licked the *frosting* off the beater.
Let it cool before you add the *frosting*.
contrast: Americans say frosting; the British say icing.

gloss: The liquid squeezed from fruit or vegetables.
examples: The *juice* is in the fridge door.
She squeezed the *juice* of two lemons.

gloss: A hot drink made by pouring boiling water over dried leaves.

countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
gloss: A sweet fizzy soft drink.
examples: Grab a couple of *sodas* from the cooler.
contrast: Called soda or pop in the US, a fizzy drink in Britain.

countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
gloss: A drink made from pressed apples.
examples: They serve hot *cider* in the fall.
He bought a gallon of *cider* at the orchard.
The *ciders* on tap are all local.
contrast: In the US cider is usually the non-alcoholic apple drink; in Britain cider is alcoholic.

gloss: A thick cold drink made from blended fruit.
examples: The banana *smoothie* is the best one.

gloss: A drink of any kind.
The food a person usually eats, or a controlled eating plan.
examples: His *diet* is mostly rice and beans.
She's been on a *diet* since January.
A balanced *diet* matters more than any single food.

gloss: A unit for measuring the energy in food.

countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
gloss: A substance in food such as meat, beans, and eggs that the body needs to build tissue.
examples: Eggs are a cheap source of *protein*.
The shake has twenty grams of *protein*.
contrast: PROH-teen — the ei is just EE, and the word has two syllables.

gloss: The part of plant food that the body cannot digest but needs.
examples: He needs more *fiber* in his diet.
The cereal box brags about its *fiber*.
contrast: American spelling fiber; British fibre. Both are said FY-bur.

gloss: A natural substance in food that the body needs in small amounts.
contrast: Americans say VY-tuh-min; the British say VIT-uh-min.
